items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I think it was Bud Scott too told me in California, that was 1940 when I talked to him in 39, maybe 1940 that winter I was there.

ctx.x: And I thought that was very interesting to hear, you know, cutting through the way he did, and you can hear the fullness of his sound on guitar.

Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. But that was part of the old New Orleans tradition, and Jelly talks about it, but Jelly also talks about they would be probably New Orleans bands, too. He was objecting to, being loud.…

Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands that the clarinet and the trumpet always were in harmony together, and the clarinet was not a counterpoint to the trumpet, but he rarely hears that now, that Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: I learned from Norwood Williams... Ori and Bud Scott and Mutt the group that were out there

ctx.x: What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case…

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz. Of course, all the young record collectors, and especially, say the ones...

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: That was the greatest rhythm section I ever heard, I'd say, was that Kid Ori rhythm section with, who's the bass player? Eddie Garland and Bud Scott and Minor Hall

ctx.x: Now these are typed in the back of the Defender notes.

Yeah. That's some of the later Defender notes, some things that I probably didn't get. He probably looked through my notes and then went up there and went through a couple of years. We'll copy all this stuff for you. So in any case, there are a few other interviews, people that are dead there like Tubby Hall and Joe Lindsay. Unfortunately, we got very little bit from Tubby Hall. I wanted to apologize on that. He was one of the great drummers, I'm convinced the more I hear of other drummers especially. At that…
